Comparison profile: BR-SP-2011 (see the comparison section).

Head loss: Hazen-Williams, h = 10.67 L Q^1.852 / (C^1.852 D^4.871). The fittings enter as equivalent length or as a sum of K. The elevations come from the elevation change of each pipe, from the nodes the reservoirs feed (elevation 0). Pressures are gauge.

The hydraulic report scenarios open each outlet with its required flow (imposed demand), and the check is the pressure the network delivers; a hydrant's hose and nozzle losses count when the requirement applies at the nozzle. When the outlet's own device is known (a K factor, a rated nozzle or a tip), the valve must also have the pressure that device needs to pass the required flow.

Fluid: water at 25.0 °C, density 997.1 kg/m³.

8. Hose reach

Every point of each protected area must be within reach of the number of nozzles the profile sets, counting the hose along its real path and the jet the profile counts. A grid of points covers each area outside the buildings, obstacles and protected risks. The reach radius (hose plus jet in a straight line) screens the points; the points it reaches are then checked along the shortest hose path around the buildings, obstacles and tanks, with the jet along the last straight leg of the path. Dikes do not stop the hose or the jet.

The available flow comes from the NFPA 291 formula, Q_R = Q_F (h_R / h_F)^0.54, with both pressure drops counted from the static pressure.

In T-01 (example readings) the pressure dropped by less than 25 % of the static, so the extrapolation to the reference residual is weak (NFPA 291 recommends a larger drop; to be checked in the text).

11. Water hammer

The transients were run by the method of characteristics (Wylie and Streeter 1993): each pipe is cut into sections a pressure wave crosses in one time step, and the friction along the characteristics is the pipe's own Hazen-Williams or Darcy-Weisbach loss at the flow of the moment, so the steady state the transient starts from is kept exactly. The wave speed of each pipe follows from the bulk modulus of the water, the wall's modulus and thickness and the way the pipe is anchored. Where the pressure falls to the vapour pressure a discrete vapour cavity forms and collapses when its volume returns to zero. A pump follows its own curve in its normal zone and the published four-quadrant data of a radial pump (Suter form) outside it, and after a trip it runs down on its inertia; the outlets discharge as emitters, their flow following the pressure.
